title: Culturally sensitive and individualised care
blurb: Give care shaped by the needs and preferences each woman identifies, use professional interpreters, avoid assumptions, and respond to health inequalities (NMC SPM, the Code, NICE).
question: Farah, 27, recently arrived in the UK as an asylum seeker and speaks Dari. At her first postnatal visit her husband offers to interpret and says she is "fine". She asks, through gestures, for a female midwife. What should the midwife do?

teach.h: Care that fits the person, not the template
teach.body: Formally: midwives must understand that women's circumstances vary widely and support, promote and protect the individual needs and preferences that women themselves identify (SPM 3.22), providing culturally sensitive, individualised care for all women, partners and families irrespective of social situation (SPM 3.27). In plain English: ask, listen and adapt. Do not assume what a woman wants because of her culture, religion, age or background; find out, and build her care around it.
teach.cite: NMC Standards of proficiency for midwives 3.22, 3.27

head: Code
What it asks of you
rows: Treat people with kindness, respect and compassion
Avoid making assumptions; recognise diversity and individual choice
Respect and uphold people's human rights
Take reasonable steps to meet language and communication needs
Use verbal and non-verbal methods; consider cultural sensitivities
Do not express personal beliefs inappropriately
teach.caption: NMC The Code (2018).

teach.h: Communicating when English is not her first language

steps.label: Identify the need
steps.sub: language, literacy, sensory or learning needs

steps.label: Professional interpreter
steps.sub: not her partner, family or friends

steps.label: Time alone with her
steps.sub: at least one consultation without her partner

teach.caption: NICE NG201 and CG110: use independent, professional interpreters; NG194 1.1.5: information translated by an appropriate interpreter and in accessible formats (digital, printed, braille, Easy Read).

teach.h: Why inequality is a safety issue
teach.body: MBRRACE-UK 2022-24 found Black women had nearly three times the maternal mortality rate of White women, and women in the most deprived areas twice that of the least deprived. NICE NG194 1.1.2 asks professionals to be aware that women and babies from some minority ethnic backgrounds and deprived areas have a higher risk of death and may need closer monitoring. Individualised care means noticing who may be at higher risk, listening when she says something is wrong, and escalating promptly.

most deprived areas vs least deprived

teach.h: Women who may need extra support (NG194 1.1.7; CG110)

children.edge: Recent migrant, asylum seeker, refugee, little English
children.label: Professional interpreter; explain services

items: Ask about her preferences: who she wants present, gender of the clinician, modesty, diet, religious or cultural practices, naming or birth customs.
Record her wishes and share them with the team so she does not have to repeat herself.
Accommodate where safe; if something cannot be met, explain why and offer alternatives.
Respect choices about feeding, cultural influences and privacy (NG194 1.5.1, 1.5.8).
Where a practice is unlawful or harmful (for example FGM of a girl under 18), follow safeguarding and legal duties: cultural sensitivity never overrides safety or the law.

teach.body: Using Farah's husband to interpret risks inaccurate information and stops her disclosing abuse, mood or other private concerns. The midwife thanks him, books a professional Dari interpreter (by phone if needed), and arranges for a female midwife where possible. She makes time to see Farah alone, asks about domestic abuse when alone, checks her understanding, and explains how to access services and who to contact. She records Farah's preferences for the whole team.

teach.text: Family members, partners and children should not act as interpreters, even when it is quicker. And cultural sensitivity does not mean accepting harm: mandatory FGM reporting for under-18s and safeguarding duties still apply.

items: Support the needs and preferences SHE identifies (SPM 3.22); care irrespective of social situation (SPM 3.27).
Code 1.3: avoid assumptions; Code 7.2-7.3: meet language needs and consider cultural sensitivities.
Use professional interpreters, not partners or family; see her alone at least once.
Black women: nearly three times the maternal death rate of White women (MBRRACE-UK 2022-24).
Respect culture and choice, but safety, safeguarding and the law come first.

summary: You can now plan care around the needs and preferences each woman identifies, communicate through professional interpreters and accessible information, and avoid assumptions. You can explain why ethnicity and deprivation affect outcomes and how individualised care responds.

A.q: Ana, 30, speaks little English. Her 14-year-old daughter offers to interpret at the postnatal visit. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Arrange a professional interpreter
Accept the daughter's help to save time
Use a translation app for the whole visit
Rely on gestures and written English
A.why: NICE NG201 and CG110 1.3.10: use a professional, independent interpreter rather than the woman's partner, family members or friends. Code 7.2: take reasonable steps to meet language needs.

whyNot.1: Children and family members should not interpret; accuracy and confidentiality suffer.
whyNot.2: A general translation app is not a professional interpreter for clinical information.
whyNot.3: Gestures and written English do not meet her communication needs safely.

A.q: Which NMC Code standard most directly asks a midwife to avoid making assumptions and to recognise diversity and individual choice?
options: Code 10.1
Code 14.1
Code 1.3
Code 18.4
A.why: Code 1.3: avoid making assumptions and recognise diversity and individual choice.

whyNot.0: Code 10.1 is about completing records at the time or as soon as possible.
whyNot.1: Code 14.1 is about acting immediately to put things right when something goes wrong.
whyNot.3: Code 18.4 is about storing medicines securely.

A.q: According to MBRRACE-UK 2022-24, how did the maternal mortality rate for Black women compare with that for White women?
options: About the same as White women
About half
About ten times as high
Nearly three times higher
A.why: MBRRACE-UK 2022-24: Black women had nearly three times the maternal mortality rate of White women.

whyNot.0: There is a large disparity, not a similar rate.
whyNot.1: The rate for Black women was higher, not lower.
whyNot.2: Ten times overstates the reported disparity.

B.q: Amira, 25, is fasting for a religious observance while breastfeeding on day 12. She asks the midwife whether she can continue. What is the best first response?
options: Tell her fasting is not permitted while breastfeeding
Advise her to switch to formula during the fast
Say it is her choice and no advice is needed
Explore her wishes and discuss staying well
B.why: SPM 3.22 and Code 1.3: explore the needs and preferences she identifies without assumptions, then give individual information so she can make an informed decision, involving religious or medical advice if she wishes.

whyNot.0: Telling her what her faith permits is an assumption and an inappropriate expression of belief (Code 20.7).
whyNot.1: Changing feeding method is not necessary advice and disregards her preferences.
whyNot.2: Respecting choice still means giving information about her health and her baby's feeding.

B.q: Shona, 17, is pregnant with her first baby. Which arrangement does NICE CG110 recommend for women under 20?
options: Referral to social care at booking
A named midwife to coordinate her care
Birth in an obstetric unit
Antenatal care through her school nurse
B.why: CG110 1.4.4: young women aged under 20 should have a named midwife who takes responsibility for and provides most of their antenatal care.

whyNot.0: Age alone is not a reason for a social care referral; safeguarding concerns would be.
whyNot.2: Age under 20 does not by itself require an obstetric unit birth.
whyNot.3: The CG110 arrangement is a named midwife, not school nursing.

B.q: During a postnatal visit, a midwife who disagrees with the couple's decision not to vaccinate their baby begins explaining her own religious view on the matter. Which Code standard is she breaching?
options: Code 13 on competence
Code 5 on confidentiality
Code 20.7 on beliefs
Code 25 on leadership
B.why: Code 20.7: do not express your personal beliefs (including political, religious or moral beliefs) to people in an inappropriate way. She should give balanced information and respect their decision.

whyNot.0: Code 13 is about working within the limits of competence.
whyNot.1: Code 5 is about privacy and confidentiality; nothing has been disclosed.
whyNot.3: Code 25 is about leadership, not personal beliefs.

C.q: Joy, 33, a Black woman, is day 4 after a caesarean. She says, "Something is not right, I feel terrible," but her early warning score is 1. Her partner says she is "just tired". What should the midwife do?
options: Take her concern seriously, reassess, escalate
Reassure her that a score of 1 means she is well
Accept her partner's view and review her tomorrow
Advise rest and recheck at the next routine visit
C.why: NG194 1.1.1 and 1.1.2: listen and respond to her needs, and be aware that women from some minority ethnic backgrounds have higher risk of death and may need closer monitoring. A woman's own sense that something is wrong warrants a full reassessment and escalation.

whyNot.1: A low score does not override her report; scores support, not replace, clinical judgement.
whyNot.2: Her own account matters; dismissing it risks missed deterioration.
whyNot.3: Delay is unsafe when a woman at higher risk reports feeling unwell.

C.q: Bisi, 28, from Nigeria, is 36 weeks pregnant. During a check the midwife sees signs of type 3 FGM. Bisi says it was done when she was a child and asks the midwife to respect her culture. She has a 4-year-old daughter. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Report Bisi to the police within one month
Respect her wishes and take no further action
Document the finding and close the matter
Record, discuss, assess risk to her daughter
C.why: For women 18 and over, FGM mandatory police reporting (FGM Act s5B) does not apply; instead a safeguarding risk assessment is needed, including risk to daughters and an unborn girl. Discuss sensitively, record, and plan birth care.

whyNot.0: Mandatory police reporting applies to girls under 18, not adult women.
whyNot.1: Respecting culture does not remove safeguarding duties towards her daughter.
whyNot.2: Recording is needed, but a safeguarding risk assessment for her daughter is also required.

C.q: Hana, 22, a wheelchair user with a hearing impairment, is planning to breastfeed. Which approach best reflects individualised care?
options: Give her the standard leaflet and helpline number
Ask her what support she needs and adapt communication
Refer her to formula feeding to avoid positioning problems
Speak to her partner, who can relay the information
C.why: SPM 3.22 and 3.27: support the needs she herself identifies. NG194 1.1.5: tailor information to her needs, in accessible formats and with communication support; Code 7.2.

whyNot.0: A standard leaflet and phone line may not meet a hearing impairment or her positioning needs.
whyNot.2: Steering her away from breastfeeding ignores her choice; positioning can be adapted.
whyNot.3: Relaying through her partner bypasses her and her right to direct communication.

reteach.title: ASK before you act
reteach.question: Individualised care can be summed up in one habit: ask before you assume. What does that habit look like in a visit?

blocks.body: Ask what matters to her and what she needs. Listen through a professional interpreter if needed, and see her alone at least once. Adapt care to her wishes where it is safe. Record her preferences so the whole team knows. If something she wants cannot be done safely or lawfully, explain why kindly and offer alternatives.

letters.word: Seek her preferences, through an interpreter if needed
Keep a record and share it with the team

blocks.text: Being culturally sensitive is not the same as assuming what a culture wants. Two women from the same community may want very different things: ask each one.

explain.body: SPM 3.22: support, promote and protect the individual needs and preferences that women themselves identify. SPM 3.27: culturally sensitive, individualised care for all women, partners and families, irrespective of social situation.

test.q: According to SPM 3.22, whose identification of needs and preferences should the midwife support and protect?
options: The midwife's own assessment
The family's elders
The woman herself
The local trust policy
test.why: SPM 3.22: support, promote and protect any individual needs and preferences that women themselves identify.

whyNot.0: Clinical assessment matters, but SPM 3.22 centres the needs the woman identifies.
whyNot.1: Family views may matter to her, but the standard refers to the woman's own preferences.
whyNot.3: Policy guides practice; the standard is about the woman's own needs.

explain.body: Use an independent, professional interpreter, not a partner, family member or friend. See the woman alone for at least one consultation. Provide information in accessible formats and check understanding.

test.q: Why should a woman's partner not act as her interpreter in a maternity consultation?
options: Partners are not permitted in any consultation
She may not feel able to disclose abuse
It breaches the Equality Act 2010
Interpreters must be medically qualified
test.why: Using a partner can prevent disclosure of domestic abuse or private concerns and risks inaccurate interpretation; NICE recommends professional interpreters and at least one consultation without the partner (CG110).

whyNot.0: Partners can be involved according to the woman's wishes (NG194 1.1.3).
whyNot.2: The Equality Act is not the reason given; the concern is disclosure and accuracy.
whyNot.3: Interpreters need to be professional, not medically qualified.

explain.body: MBRRACE-UK 2022-24: maternal mortality 12.80 per 100,000; Black women nearly three times the rate of White women; most deprived areas twice the least deprived. NG194 1.1.2: be aware some groups may need closer monitoring.

test.q: What does NICE NG194 1.1.2 ask professionals to do in response to higher maternal and neonatal mortality in some groups?
options: Be aware they may need closer monitoring
Transfer all such women to consultant care
Offer them an extra scan at 36 weeks
Discharge them later from hospital
test.why: NG194 1.1.2: be aware that women and babies from some minority ethnic backgrounds and those in deprived areas have an increased risk of death and may need closer monitoring.

whyNot.1: NICE does not recommend routine transfer to consultant care on this basis.
whyNot.2: An extra 36-week scan is not the NG194 recommendation.
whyNot.3: Delayed discharge is not the recommended response; closer monitoring is.

explain.body: Accommodate cultural and religious preferences where safe, explain kindly when something cannot be done, and remember legal and safeguarding duties still apply, for example FGM reporting for girls under 18 and risk assessment for daughters of adult women with FGM.

test.q: Mia, 26, asks that only female staff examine her for religious reasons. What is the best response?
options: Explain that staff cannot be chosen on the NHS
Agree, but tell her this will delay all care
Ask her to bring a family member to chaperone instead
Record her wish; arrange female staff if possible
test.why: SPM 3.22 and Code 1.3: respect and record her identified preference and accommodate it where possible; in an emergency, explain if this cannot be met and why.

whyNot.0: Refusing outright ignores her identified need; preferences should be accommodated where possible.
whyNot.1: Threatening delay is not respectful and is not accurate for most care.
whyNot.2: A chaperone does not meet her preference for female staff.
